title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
authors: Edward J. Hu, Yelong Shen, Phillip Wallis, Zeyuan Allen-Zhu, Yuanzhi Li, Shean Wang, Lu Wang, Weizhu Chen

pages.title: Freeze the big model, train tiny low-rank adapters

blocks.html: Full fine-tuning of a 175B-parameter model means storing and updating 175B parameters per task. That's expensive in compute, expensive in memory, and impossible to deploy at scale (you'd need a full model copy per downstream task).

LoRA's idea: freeze the pre-trained weights $W$ entirely. For each weight matrix you'd otherwise fine-tune, learn a low-rank update $\Delta W = B A$ where $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}$ and $A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}$, with $r \ll \min(d, k)$. At inference: $h = (W + BA)x$. The forward pass through $W$ stays unchanged; only $A$ and $B$ are trained.
LoRA can reduce the number of trainable parameters by 10,000× and the GPU memory requirement by 3×, while performing on par or better than fine-tuning on RoBERTa, DeBERTa, GPT-2, and GPT-3.
Headline numbers for GPT-3 175B: trainable params drop from 175B → 4.7M (≈10000× fewer), checkpoint size 350GB → 35MB, no added inference latency once $BA$ is merged into $W$.

Pre-train-then-fine-tune is the standard transfer learning recipe. But as base models cross 100B parameters, fine-tuning becomes operationally hostile: every downstream task needs its own copy of the model, and the optimizer state (Adam's moment estimates) requires ~2× the parameter memory on top of the weights themselves.

Earlier parameter-efficient methods — adapter layers (Houlsby et al.) and prefix tuning (Li & Liang) — reduce trainable parameters, but adapters add inference latency (extra sequential layers) and prefix tuning is hard to optimize and reduces usable sequence length.

Aghajanyan et al. showed empirically that pre-trained language models have a low intrinsic dimension: the task-specific update needed to solve a downstream task can be represented in a much smaller subspace than the full parameter space.
LoRA takes the next step: if the update $\Delta W$ is intrinsically low-rank, parameterize it that way explicitly. Use $\Delta W = BA$ with rank $r$, and you've matched the hypothesized structure.
For a pre-trained weight $W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$, the LoRA update is:

blocks.tex: W_0 + \Delta W = W_0 + B A,\quad B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r},\; A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k},\; r \ll \min(d, k)

blocks.html: $W_0$ is frozen (no gradient). Only $A$ and $B$ are trained. The forward pass becomes:

blocks.tex: h = W_0 x + B A x

blocks.html: Initialization: $A$ is initialized to a random Gaussian, $B$ is initialized to zero. So at the start of training, $\Delta W = BA = 0$ and the model behaves exactly like the frozen base — fine-tuning starts from the pre-trained model and can only improve from there.
Scaling: the update is scaled by $\alpha / r$ where $\alpha$ is a constant. This makes the update invariant to changes in $r$: doubling $r$ doesn't double the magnitude of $\Delta W$.

pages.title: Which weights to adapt? Where to put LoRA

blocks.html: In a Transformer, you could LoRA-fy any weight matrix: the four attention projections ($W_q, W_k, W_v, W_o$), the two FFN matrices, or all of them.

Empirically, adapting just $W_q$ and $W_v$ (the query and value projections) gives the best parameter-budget-to-quality tradeoff. Adapting $W_k$ adds little; the FFN matrices benefit somewhat but are huge.

No inference latency: once trained, you can absorb $BA$ directly into $W_0$ by computing $W = W_0 + BA$ once. The deployed model has identical shape to the original. (You can also keep them separate if you need to swap tasks.)

LoRA is benchmarked against full fine-tuning, adapters (multiple variants), prefix tuning, and BitFit on RoBERTa-base/large, DeBERTa-XXL, GPT-2 medium/large, and GPT-3 175B. Tasks: GLUE, WikiSQL, MNLI, SAMSum, E2E NLG.

items: RoBERTa large on GLUE: LoRA with 0.8M params matches full fine-tuning (355M params) average score.
GPT-3 175B on WikiSQL: LoRA with 4.7M params reaches 73.4% — exceeds full fine-tuning (73.8%) within noise, while prefix tuning lags by 2-4 points.
GPT-3 175B on MNLI-m: LoRA 91.7%, full FT 89.5%. LoRA actually beats full FT here, likely due to the regularization effect of constraining updates to low rank.

pages.title: Why does it work? Investigating the low-rank update

blocks.html: Section 7 of the paper digs into what the LoRA update is capturing. They find:

items: Even rank r=1 or r=2 already captures most of the task-specific signal. r=8 is rarely improved on. This validates the low-intrinsic-rank claim.

$\Delta W$ amplifies directions in $W$ that the pre-trained model wasn't already emphasizing — i.e. it highlights task-relevant features that were latent but underused, rather than rotating the model entirely.
The amplification factor is large: $\Delta W$ has features whose magnitude is ~20× larger than the corresponding directions in $W$ itself.

blocks.html: LoRA is now the default parameter-efficient fine-tuning method in open-source ecosystems (HuggingFace PEFT, etc). Reasons:

items: Trivially composable — multiple LoRAs can be added together to combine tasks/styles.
Storage and switching costs collapse: a 7B model + 10 LoRAs takes ~14GB instead of 140GB.
Works as well as full fine-tuning in most regimes, sometimes better.

blocks.html: QLoRA (next paper) extends this by quantizing the frozen base to 4-bit, making LoRA fine-tuning of 65B+ models possible on a single consumer GPU.
